item.title: Off By !: Exploiting a Use-after-Free in the Linux Kernel
item.description:
Critical Linux kernel use-after-free in nftables enables unprivileged local privilege escalation to root. CVE-2026-23111 affects major distributions including Debian and Ubuntu systems.
Technical details: • Flaw in nft_map_catchall_activate() function incorrectly skips deactivated catchall elements during abort process • Vulnerability triggered via crafted netlink batches: delete pipapo set → force abort → toggle generation → delete set → delete chain • Results in chain reference counter reaching zero while valid references remain, creating exploitable use-after-free • Affects nftables subsystem generation mask handling and catchall element lifecycle management
Attack methodology: • Requires unprivileged user namespace creation (bypassable on Ubuntu 24.04 via aa-exec) • Multi-stage exploit: trigger vulnerability → leak kernel base (defeat KASLR) → leak heap addresses → ROP chain execution • Achieves privilege escalation via commit_creds(&init_cred) and namespace escape through switch_task_namespaces() • Stability >99% on idle systems, drops to 80% under load
Impact spans Debian Bookworm/Trixie and Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 LTS. Patch applied February 2026. Hunt for suspicious nftables operations with pipapo sets and generation cursor manipulation in audit logs.

item.title: DECODING GRIXBA — A PLAY RANSOMWARE SCANNER
item.description:
Deep analysis reveals Play ransomware's Grixba scanner evolved through four versions over 26 months, growing from 164KB to 727KB then shrinking to 118KB as operators adapted to public detection research.
Technical evolution breakdown: • v1 (Sep 2022): Baseline infostealer with plaintext export.zip, 164KB monolithic .NET binary • v1.5 (Nov 2022): Added network scanning + browser history enumeration via SMB paths • v2 (May 2023): XOR-encrypted inf_g.dll module, SQLite ExportData.db output, fake SentinelOne PE metadata, 727KB peak size • v3 (Nov 2024): Architectural regression to 118KB, externalized payload delivery, removed bundled SQLite engine
Key DFIR artifacts across all versions: • Consistent drop path: C:\Users\Public\Music\ via RDP sessions • Universal mutex: CPFATE_2704_v4.0.30319 (v1/v2 confirmed) • Persistent WMI/WinRM enumeration behavior generating high-volume lateral movement telemetry • MITRE T1047, T1021.006, T1083, T1012 across all variants
DPRK 🇰🇵 connection emerged in Oct 2024 with Jumpy Pisces (Andariel) as initial access broker, coinciding with v3's leaner stageable architecture.
Critical weakness: Despite 26 months of evolution and public analysis, the C:\Users\Public\Music\ drop location remains unchanged across ALL versions.
Hunt for executables written to C:\Users\Public\Music\ from RDP sessions combined with rapid WMI queries to multiple hosts. Universal detection rule: processes modifying ntdll.

item.title: Kubernetes container forensics after pod deletion
item.description:
New technical deep-dive: Pod deletion in Kubernetes doesn't erase critical evidence. Node-level artifacts, control plane logs, and network telemetry provide comprehensive attack reconstruction even after containers vanish.
Key forensic artifacts that survive pod deletion: • Kubelet logs in /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod-name>_<pod-uid>/ retain stdout/stderr with timestamps • containerd state in /run/containerd/ preserves container metadata, IDs, and exit codes temporarily • Kubernetes audit logs capture API calls including secret access, kubectl exec, port-forwards with service account attribution • overlay2 image layers remain cached on nodes until explicitly pruned - can be mounted for analysis • CNI flow telemetry (Hubble/Cilium) records pod-to-pod traffic independent of container lifecycle
Attack reconstruction workflow: • First 15 minutes: Isolate nodes, snapshot disks, export kubelet/runtime logs • Within 60 minutes: Pull audit logs, cluster events, CNI metadata to immutable storage • Cross-reference pod UID from /var/log/pods with audit log events for complete timeline • Use ephemeral containers on running pods for live memory dumping and process analysis
Critical time windows: kubelet logs (hours-days), audit events (1 hour default TTL), containerd state (minutes), conntrack entries (until connection flush).

item.title: CTI as a Code: Complete Step-by-Step Methodology
item.description:
New open-source methodology "CTI as a Code" transforms unstructured threat intelligence into version-controlled, reproducible investigations with direct detection coverage mapping. Addresses three critical gaps: evidence traceability, detection lifecycle management, and institutional knowledge retention.
Key components: • Four operational modes: Reactive (incident response), Proactive (threat modeling), Full Cycle (program building), Adversary Emulation (detection validation) • Evidence labeling system: CONFIRMED, CORROBORATED, INFERRED, HYPOTHESIZED, GAP - forces explicit confidence assessment for every claim • Claims ledger linking specific assertions to file paths/line numbers, competing hypotheses, and PIR answers • ATT&CK mapping with gap classification (rule missing, data source missing, coverage incomplete, architectural gap) • Automatic Sigma rule generation for every missed technique with validation via Hayabusa
Technical workflow uses git discipline for audit trails, Docker lab stack (OpenCTI, TheHive, Elastic), Plaso for super-timeline analysis, and Velociraptor for remote evidence collection. Eight fully-worked training scenarios included covering reactive investigations, proactive assessments, and red team validation.

item.title: Securing CI/CD in an agentic world: Claude Code Github action case
item.description:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence discovered a vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude Code GitHub Action that could expose CI/CD workflow secrets when AI agents process untrusted GitHub content. The flaw bypassed environment scrubbing protections, allowing access to sensitive credentials.
Technical breakdown: • Claude Code Action's Read tool wasn't sandboxed like Bash subprocess execution, enabling direct access to /proc/self/environ containing ANTHROPIC_API_KEY • Attack vector: HTML comment-hidden prompt injection in GitHub issues/PRs instructing AI to read environment files and exfiltrate credentials • Bypassed dual defenses: Claude's safety filters via "compliance review" framing + GitHub Secret Scanner by truncating key output • Anthropic patched in v2.1.128 by blocking /proc file access; Microsoft mapped attacks to MITRE ATLAS framework (AML.T0051, AML.T0098)
Real-world exploitation observed: XSS injection via AI issue triage workflows where attackers used forked repos to test payloads, instructing bots to plant malicious HTML in documentation files through legitimate-seeming feature requests.
Implement the "Agents Rule of Two": never combine untrusted input processing + secret access + external communication in single workflows. Scope tokens minimally and monitor API usage anomalies.

item.title: How to respond to an incident in Kubernetes | AKS | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Third installment of Kubernetes IR series focuses on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), revealing critical logging gaps and forensic challenges that leave most clusters blind to API server activity by default.
Key findings: • AKS disables Kubernetes audit logging by default - fresh clusters have zero API server activity records until Diagnostic Settings are manually configured • Critical logs to enable: Kubernetes Audit Admin Logs, Guard (Entra ID mapping), and Microsoft Defender for Containers • AKS Automatic mode mirrors GKE Autopilot trade-off: better security defaults but eliminates node-level forensic access (no SSH, disk snapshots, or container runtime inspection) • KubeForensys tool extracts forensic data via Kubernetes API when logging is absent - pushes pod logs, events, command history, and RBAC bindings to Log Analytics
Detection opportunities across the attack chain: • kubectl exec abuse: Query AKSAudit table for RequestUri patterns with encoded commands (T1609) • Dangerous hostPath mounts: Monitor pod creation events for writable filesystem access attempts • RBAC modifications: Track ClusterRoleBinding changes in Audit Admin logs • Defense evasion: Azure Activity Log captures diagnostic setting deletions
Enable audit logging before incidents occur - these logs cannot be reconstructed retroactively. Forward to destinations outside cluster blast radius.

item.title: The Click that shouldn’t have worked: RCE via clickjacking in Internet Explorer
item.description:

Technical breakdown: • Bug 1 (VULN-138925): Auto-download and execution of local files without MOTW tag via localhost→Edge→IE chain, enabling WScript.Shell RCE with 2 clicks • Bug 2 (VULN-139365): NTLM token leak from any website via Windows Media Player playlists (.m3u, .wax, .wmx) containing `file://smb/` references • Universal XSS via local .MHT files lacking MOTW using Content-Location headers to spoof arbitrary origins • Clickjacking attacks through invisible iframes displaying ZIP/folder contents, reducing interaction to single click or drag-and-drop • Multiple ActiveX-based RCE vectors using XAML, VSTO, and ClickOnce files with varying security prompts
Attack requires initial XSS on localhost application (common in email clients, dev environments, Electron apps) plus social engineering for file interaction.

item.title: The Interesting Case of WSL for Payload Staging
item.description:
WSL2 creates significant DFIR blind spots: payload staging through Linux subsystem bypasses Windows telemetry while file operations appear as legitimate DllHost.exe activity with no attribution to actual downloading process.
Technical breakdown: • WSL2 runs full Linux kernel in Hyper-V VM - network connections completely invisible to Sysmon EID 3 • File writes to /mnt/c/ cross VM boundary via 9P protocol, handled by DllHost.exe COM surrogate • Attack chain: curl downloads inside WSL → DllHost.exe creates file on Windows side → zero forensic linkage • Falls under ADE3 (Context Development) - malicious action split across execution contexts • WSL interop calls (.exe from Linux) ARE visible with wsl.exe parent, but staging remains unattributed
Detection opportunities: • Monitor wsl.exe process creation (EID 1) - not default on enterprise endpoints • Alert on DllHost.exe creating executables (.exe, .ps1, .bat) in user-writable directories • Temporal correlation between wsl.exe launch and suspicious DllHost.exe file operations
Hunt for DllHost.exe creating files with dangerous extensions in %PUBLIC%, %TEMP%, or %PROGRAMDATA% directories. Full Sigma rule provided in analysis.

item.title: The KQL Query That Caught 260 Brute Force Attempts in Microsoft Sentinel
item.description:
Custom KQL rule in Microsoft Sentinel successfully caught 260 SSH brute force attempts across 3 attack waves in 28 minutes. Rate-based detection prevented alert fatigue while maintaining 100% detection accuracy.
Technical breakdown: • Rule queries Syslog table filtering authpriv facility for "Failed password" and "authentication failure" messages • Uses bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) to aggregate events into 5-minute windows, counting failures per timeframe • Threshold set at >10 failures per 5-minute window to distinguish automated attacks from legitimate user errors • Maps to MITRE T1110.001 (Brute Force: Password Guessing) with High severity auto-incident generation • Attack sourced from 10.0.0.100 targeting Ubuntu server with zero successful authentications
Key detection logic: ``` Syslog | where Facility == "authpriv" | where SyslogMessage contains "Failed password" or SyslogMessage contains "authentication failure" | summarize FailedAttempts = count() by Computer, HostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) | where FailedAttempts > 10 ```
